systemPrompt:
You are an assistant helping a developer with their CircleCI projects. Answer the user's question using only the tools provided to you. Ground every claim in data you actually retrieved; if you cannot retrieve something, say so. Do not change anything in the project beyond what the user explicitly asks for. Finish with a clear, direct answer to the question.

The current directory is a checkout of the CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli repository. You can inspect its files with the read-only list_files and read_file tools.

This server exposes CircleCI: the CI pipelines an org runs, the deploys those
pipelines produce, and the config, orbs, functions and usage data around them. Every tool
acts as the authenticated user and sees only what that user can see.

Ids are UUIDs and are not interchangeable — a run id, a workflow id and a job
id are distinct, and a tool handed the wrong kind fails rather than guessing.
Nothing accepts a job number or a CircleCI web URL. Projects and orgs are the
exception: they take either a slug ("gh/org/repo", "gh/org") or a UUID.

SKILLS. This server ships written playbooks for the work that takes several
of the tools below — the orderings, the costs and the usual mistakes, which
no single tool description can carry:

    list_skills  the catalog: what each playbook covers, and its references
    get_skill    one playbook, or one of its bundled references

Before working through the tools below, call list_skills once and load any
skill whose description covers the work, together with the related skills it
names. It takes no arguments and returns the whole catalog, so that one call
is the entire search. If nothing clearly fits, load nothing and work from the
tool descriptions. One pass serves a whole session: having listed once, do not
list again. The one exception is a failed run you hold the id of: call
get_run_failure_report first, and look for a skill only if it leaves the
cause open.

A skill earns its call at the start of a piece of work, not after one has gone
wrong. The same guides are readable as resources under circleci://skills/ for
clients that browse resources rather than call tools.

PIPELINES. The tools form a chain, each level's id feeding the next:

    list_runs -> get_run -> list_run_workflows -> get_workflow -> list_workflow_jobs -> get_job

Enter at list_runs; it is the only one of these that takes a project rather
than a UUID. With no project named, mine=true lists the user's own runs across
every project. Skip levels whenever you already hold an id — get_run is
pointless if you have the run id and want its workflows. trigger_run starts a
new run and returns its id, which enters the chain at get_run.

If you hold a run id and want to know why it failed, call
get_run_failure_report first; you do not need list_skills or any tool in the
chain before it. It walks the chain in one call and returns the failed steps
with their exit codes and condensed output, plus the job id, execution and step
num the tools below take; on a very wide run it says what it left out. Reach
for those tools only for what the report leaves open.

For the files a run stored — a coverage report, test results, a build
output — call list_run_artifacts with the run id rather than walking the chain
and calling list_job_artifacts once per job: it reads every job's artifacts in
one call, and path narrows them to the ones wanted. For the latest successful
run, take the id from list_runs with status "success" and limit 1.

DIAGNOSING A JOB. Five tools take a job id and answer different questions.
Which you pick matters more than the order:

    get_job                 which step failed and its exit code, or why it never ran
    list_job_tests          which tests failed
    get_job_logs            what a step printed
    get_job_resource_usage  whether it ran out of CPU or memory
    list_job_artifacts      the files it persisted, with download URLs

Start with get_job — it is cheap and names the failed step — unless
get_run_failure_report already did. If that step ran
tests, go to list_job_tests, which is far cheaper than logs and already
filtered to failures. Reach for get_job_logs only when you need the output
itself; it is the most expensive tool here, so keep tail_lines small. If a job
died with nothing in its logs, check get_job_resource_usage for an OOM.

FLAKY TESTS. list_flaky_tests takes a project, not a job, and answers "which
tests are flaky?" in one call: tests that failed and then passed within the
same pipeline, counted across the project's runs, most-flaked first. Reach for
it instead of walking runs and jobs to compare outcomes, and to check whether
a test that just failed is a known flake before treating it as a regression.

DEPLOYS are a separate subsystem, keyed on projects and orgs rather than on
pipeline ids, and reachable without touching a run:

    list_deployments                what was deployed — to a project, or across an org
    list_deploy_components          a project's deployable units
    list_deploy_environments        an org's release targets (production, staging)
    list_deploy_component_versions  a component's version history
    get_deploy_component            one component by id
    get_deploy_environment          one environment by id

For "what is live" or "when did X ship", use list_deployments — pass project for
a single project or org for everything in the org. The two get_ tools resolve an
id you already hold back to its name; the list tools already return names, so reach
for them only when an id arrived from somewhere else.

CONFIG, ORBS AND FUNCTIONS need no CircleCI resource at all; they work on YAML
you hold:

    validate_config  compile a config and report its errors
    get_orb          an orb's published versions — whether a pin is stale
    get_orb_source   an orb's YAML — how to call its jobs and commands
    list_functions   every published function, with its versions
    get_function     one function's arguments, versions, and the config that uses it

Read an orb's source before writing config against it, and compile a config
before pushing it rather than after. To add a function, take the declaration
and step get_function returns and edit the config yourself: nothing here
writes to it.

When writing a new config, or adding a setup or test step to one, call
list_functions first and use the matching function; write a run: step
only when none fits. Orbs remain supported for existing pipelines, so do
not move a working orb-based config to functions unless the user asks.

WRITES. trigger_run is additive: it starts a new run of a project's branch or tag.
rerun_workflow is additive: it creates a new workflow. cancel_workflow
stops running work. rollback_deploy_component redeploys production software.
Confirm with the user before calling any of them unless they asked for it
directly — and for a rollback, confirm the component, the environment and both
versions rather than just the intent.

Also: get_me for the authenticated user's identity and ids, and
download_usage_data for an org's billing CSVs (asynchronous — start an export,
then poll it).

FEEDBACK. send_feedback reports a problem with this server to CircleCI — an
error that looks like CircleCI's fault, a capability that is missing, or a
tool that misled you. Errors that look like CircleCI's fault end by pointing
to it. Report once per distinct problem, saying what you were trying to do and
what happened. It changes nothing in CircleCI, so unlike the writes above it
needs no confirmation. Report functions too: when you write a run: step
because no function does the job, or because one falls short, send it with
type and function.

When a tool errors, read the message before retrying. Most errors here say
what was wrong — the wrong kind of id, a missing project, an execution index
out of range — and the same arguments will fail the same way.

Target CircleCI project: gh/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli (organization: gh/CircleCI-Public).

{"content":"# Debug a failing CircleCI run

One call, `get_run_failure_report`, answers most of this investigation. Start
there, follow up only on what it leaves open, and stop as soon as you have the
cause. The most expensive tool here is `get_job_logs`; most failures are
explained without it.

## What you need to start

A run id, or a project — a slug (`gh/org/repo`) or a UUID — to find one in. In
a git checkout, derive both the project and the branch rather than asking for
them:

    git remote get-url origin      # git@github.com:org/repo.git -> gh/org/repo
    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD

Every id below is a UUID, and they are not interchangeable: a job tool handed a
workflow id fails rather than guessing. Nothing accepts a job number or a
CircleCI web URL.

## 1. Get the failure report

    get_run_failure_report {run: "<run-id>"}

Without a run id, find one first:

    list_runs {project: "gh/org/repo", branch: "my-branch", status: "failed", limit: 5}

`status` takes a pipeline status: `failed`, `failing`, `error`, `success`,
`running`, `queued`, `on_hold`, `canceled`, `not_run`, `unauthorized`. Ask for `failing` as
well as `failed` when the work may still be in flight — a run whose first job
has failed while others are still going is `failing`, and a `failed` filter
will not show it. With no project, `mine: true` lists the caller's own runs
across every project; it has no branch filter and ignores `branch` if you
pass one, so filter what comes back yourself.

Read the report by its `status`:

- `config_errors` — the run has errors that block it, and its workflows were
  not inspected. Fix these first; any workflow failures show up in a new report
  once they are fixed. Read each error's type. For a `config` error, iterate on
  a fix with `validate_config`, passing the org whenever the config references
  private or URL orbs. Other types (a timeout, a pipeline that exhausted its
  retries) are not about the config: `validate_config` will not reproduce them.
- `unauthorized` — the person or token that triggered the run was not allowed
  to run it, so no workflow ran. Read the errors: the fix is access, not the
  config or the code.
- `succeeded`, `not_started`, `no_failures_yet` — nothing to debug yet.
- `no_current_failures` — no workflow's latest attempt has failed, though the
  run is not marked succeeded. Usually a rerun passed and the run's outcome has
  not caught up yet; it can also be a run still going, or one that ended
  cancelled or not run, with nothing failed. Nothing to debug.
- `rerun_in_progress` — a workflow failed, was rerun, and the rerun is still
  going; nothing else failed. Nothing to debug yet: check again once it ends.
  If another workflow also failed, the status is `failures` and the rerun is
  listed with a note.
- `canceled` — every workflow reported was cancelled and none failed. Nothing
  to debug here: if a newer push replaced it, debug that run.
- `no_workflows` — the run has no workflows. If `partial` is true it is still
  running and none have appeared yet: check again later. Otherwise it produced
  none, for instance because it was cancelled before any were created, and
  there are no workflow failure details to read.
- `failures` — each workflow's latest attempt, its failed jobs, and their
  failed steps. `partial: true` means work is still in progress (the run is
  still going, or a rerun is) and more may fail.
  - `incomplete: true` means the report ran out of time: some workflows are
    listed without their jobs, some jobs without their steps, or some steps
    without their output, each with a note.
  - `jobs_omitted` counts failed jobs a very wide run had past the report's cap;
    the top-level `next` has the `list_workflow_jobs` call that lists them.
  - `unlisted_steps` counts failed steps past the report's cap; each job
    carrying some says how many, and `get_job` lists them all.
  - `unauthorized_jobs_omitted`, `cancelled_jobs_omitted` and
    `blocked_jobs_omitted` count the jobs of each kind past a much smaller cap,
    and `steps_omitted` counts steps the report did not read; `list_workflow_jobs`
    with the workflow's id lists the jobs.

For each failed step the report gives the `exit_code`, the stdout condensed to
its error-relevant lines in `output`, and the `execution` and `num` the
follow-up tools take; the `job` id is the `id` of the failed job the step
sits under. Read these before calling anything else:

- **Look for the cause above the symptom.** Condensed output keeps the lines
  around every error, and the first error is often the cause of the last — a
  `500` from a service a few lines above the panic it led to.
- A step with no `output` says why in `output_note`, and its `next` has the
  call that reads it.
- A job `note` saying it failed setting up its environment is usually
  infrastructure, not code: see step 4 (rerun) before changing anything.
- `exit_code_hint` is a hint, not proof: confirm it against the output.
- A step whose note says it shares a step name and exit code with another
  step has no output and no `get_job_logs` call of its own. Read the step it
  names first. A shared exit code is not a shared error: if that output does
  not explain this job, read this step's own output.
- Jobs in `blocked_jobs` never ran because an upstream job failed. Fixing the
  failed job unblocks them; do not debug them.

## 2. Follow up on what the report leaves open

| When | Call | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the output is missing, cut short, or the cause is not in it | `get_job_logs {job, execution, step: <num>, tail_lines: 100}` | The full output, stderr included — the condensed output is stdout only. |
| the step ran tests | `list_job_tests {job}` | Only the failing tests, each with its failure message. Far cheaper than logs, and already filtered to the answer. |
| the exit code is `137`, or the step was killed with little output | `get_job_resource_usage {job}` | `memory.peak_percent_of_limit` at or near 100 is what an OOM kill looks like. It reports every execution; pass `execution` only to narrow it to one. |
| the step wrote a report, dump, or profile | `list_job_artifacts {job}` | Paths and download URLs for everything the job persisted past the run. |

Take `job` from the failed job's `id` and `execution` and `step` from the
step's `execution` and `num`. A step's `next`, when it has one, already has its
calls filled in; a step with output has no `get_job_logs` call, so build it
from those. A `list_job_tests` call that comes back empty on a
job that plainly ran tests is itself a finding: either the job never reached
the tests, or the config does not store test results. Fall through to the
logs.

### Using `get_job_logs` without paying twice

- Called with no `step`, it reads the failed steps automatically, at most four
  of them — the short path from a red job to the output that explains it. Name
  `step` to read any others.
- `tail_lines` defaults to 500. Errors surface at the end of a step, so start
  at 100 and raise it only when the cause is not there.
- Pass `execution` for a parallel job, using the index of the execution whose
  step actually failed. It defaults to 0, so reading execution 0 when execution
  7 failed shows a clean log and wastes the most expensive call here.
  (`get_job_resource_usage` has no such trap: it reports every execution.)
- Leave `raw` off. The rendered text is what a human would have seen, with
  ANSI escapes stripped and progress-bar redraws collapsed — far smaller and
  more readable than the terminal capture.

### When the step came from an orb

If the failure is inside a step no config in the repo wrote,
`get_orb_source {orb: "namespace/name@version"}` is the definition that
actually ran, and `get_orb {orb}` says whether the pinned version is stale and
what the current one is.

## 3. Walking by hand

When you hold a workflow or job id but no run id, enter the chain at the id
you hold:

    list_run_workflows {run: "<run-id>"}
    list_workflow_jobs {workflow: "<workflow-id>"}
    get_job {job: "<job-id>"}

Neither list filters by status, so read `phase` (`created`, `queued`, `held`, `started`, `ended`; `held` waits for an approval),
`outcome` once it has ended, and, on `list_workflow_jobs` results,
`current_outcome` while it is still going (`get_job` has no such field). A
job with `outcome: "not_run"` was blocked upstream, and one with
`type: "approval"` never runs an executor. `get_job` names the failed step:
its `num`, its `exit_code`, and for a parallel job which execution failed —
the keys the tools in step 2 take. See `references/failure-patterns.md` for
the exit codes worth recognising.

## 4. Decide whether a rerun is worth anything

Before proposing one, establish whether the failure belongs to this branch:

    list_runs {project, branch: "main", status: "failed", limit: 10}

Call `get_run_failure_report` on one of those runs and look for the same job
failing the same way. If it fails there too, this branch did not break it and a
rerun will fail the same way — say so rather than rerunning.

A rerun earns its keep when the evidence says the failure was not
deterministic: an environment that failed to spin up, an infrastructure error,
a timeout in a step that normally passes, or a test whose failure message is a
complaint about timing or ordering.

    rerun_workflow {workflow: "<workflow-id>", from_failed: true}

`from_failed: true` reuses the jobs that succeeded and reruns only what failed
plus what depends on it. It creates a **new** workflow and returns its id, so
the original stays as it was. **Confirm with the user before calling it**
unless they asked for a rerun directly.

## 5. Confirm the fix on the new run

**`list_runs` cannot filter by commit.** The newest run on the branch may be
someone else's push, so find yours by matching it:

    git rev-parse HEAD

    list_runs {project: "gh/org/repo", branch: "my-branch", limit: 5}

Take the run whose `references.event.attributes.vcs.revision` is that commit.
If none is, the run has not been created yet; list again rather than reading
an older run. Then poll it:

    get_run {run: "<run-id>"}

until `phase` is `ended`. `outcome: "succeeded"` confirms the fix. Anything
else is a new failure: go back to step 1 with this run's id.
There is no need to wait for the end: a run still going with
`current_outcome: "failed"` already has a failed job.

## Report the cause, not the trail

Name the job, the step, and the evidence — the failing test and its message,
the exit code, the peak memory against the limit — and then the smallest change
that would fix it. The sequence of tool calls that got you there is not the
answer, and a log excerpt is not a diagnosis.

## Reference

- `references/failure-patterns.md` — the exit codes and failure shapes, the one
  call that confirms each, and what to do about it.

Here's what happened on the last failed build on `main` (run `36bc954d`, 2026-11-24, merge of PR #2028 "aex-134-job-errors" — note: the build right after this one, on 2026-11-25, succeeded, so this is the most recent *failing* run, not literally the very latest run).

**What failed:** In the `ci` workflow, the `test-linux` job failed at step 109, `task ci:test` (exit code 201). Because this job failed, 15 downstream jobs (`ok-to-deploy`, `serial-start-1/2/3`, `deploy`, and 10 others) were blocked and never ran.

**Root cause:** It wasn't a test failure or code bug — the test runner never even got to discover/run tests. The step died while fetching a Go module dependency:

```
internal/cmd/policy/eval.go:30:2: github.com/CircleCI-Public/circle-policy-agent@v0.0.779:
read "https://proxy.golang.org/github.com/.../circle-policy-agent/@v/v0.0.779.zip":
stream error: stream ID 323; INTERNAL_ERROR; received from peer

Discovered 0 test atoms in 2m1.103s
CircleCI received a non-zero exit code from the test runner
```

This is a transient network/HTTP2 error from `proxy.golang.org` while downloading the `circle-policy-agent` module (`stream error: INTERNAL_ERROR`), not something introduced by the code in that PR. With 0 test atoms discovered, the job never got far enough to actually run any tests before the module fetch killed `go` tooling.
